name: Daria Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get in around nine, make tea, and read the overnight error alerts from Routewise, the route-planning software we sell to delivery firms. Most of my day is fixing small bugs in old Java code nobody else wants to touch, like why a van in one city got sent the long way round. Priya, the senior developer who looks after me, reviews my changes in the afternoon and usually sends a few back. I'm slower than the others on my team, I know that, but I'm careful.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a bug finally makes sense, when you see the one line that's wrong. What wears me out is the pressure to use the AI coding assistant everyone else has switched on. My manager brings it up at every check-in, and I keep saying I'd rather understand what I write. I've never used it, not once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, at least in our tech workers' union chat. A lot of bosses promised it would change everything, and it turned into a fancy autocomplete. I'd post that the hype was mostly used to scare people into accepting smaller pay rises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but not completely. Even in a plateau, the people using the tool would do tests and small fixes faster than me. The routine bits of coding are exactly the work juniors like me get handed, so I'd still feel a bit squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going much as I am, and keep putting a fifth of my pay aside every month, like I already do. I'd finally take the Java course work keeps offering, because being slow is a bigger risk to me than any robot. I wouldn't touch the assistant unless I was told I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a small knot underneath. I've got about nine months of savings, so I'm not scared for the rent. But I'd know I was still the slowest person on the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your manager raises the assistant at every check-in. In this world, does that pressure go away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not fully. If the tool saves people an hour a day, my manager will still ask why I don't use it. I'd have to show my work is good enough without it, which means getting better faster than I have been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and your partner talk about at dinner, if this is how it went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Ines is a nurse on nights, so our dinner is often her breakfast. She'd tell me to stop worrying about my job and look at her ward, which is always short of staff. She'd be right, too: nursing has problems no chatbot is going to fix.

say: I'd say the **hype** turned out to be little more than a fancy autocomplete.
I'd post that bosses used the hype to keep **pay rises** small.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, but not completely safe.
Colleagues with the tool would still speed through the **routine work** juniors like me get.
do: Keep **saving** a fifth of every paycheck, as I already do.
Take the company's **Java course** this year so I stop being the slowest.
Avoid the **AI assistant** unless my manager makes it compulsory.
feel: Mostly **relief**, with a small knot about being the **slowest** on the team.
S0.quote: The routine bits of coding are exactly the work juniors like me get handed, so I'd still feel a bit squeezed.
fieldNote: Her real fear in this world is her **own pace**, not the technology.
She reads AI hype as a tool used against **workers' pay**.
Nine months of **savings** keep the rent off her mind entirely.
Her partner's **nursing job** keeps her own worries in proportion.

steps.text: Keep fixing routing bugs in the old Java services
Put a fifth of each paycheck into savings
Finish the company's Java course before spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd keep my head down, but in the union chat I'd push hard for rules on how these tools get used. Things like no one losing their job to a tool without a proper consultation, and juniors still getting trained. Online I'd say this is a choice companies are making, not the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm the obvious one to cut. I'm junior, I'm slower than average, and I'm the only one who won't use the tool. If they stop hiring juniors and one of us goes, it's me. I can see that clear as anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union group at Routewise to ask for a written agreement on training and no cuts without notice. I'd grudgingly learn the assistant, just enough to not be the odd one out by the summer. And I'd stop the holiday fund and put that into savings instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry. I chose this work because it's quiet and logical, and now the logic is being done by something else. I've got the money to get through a year without pay, but I don't have a plan for what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me first, honestly, and then Tobi, the other junior. He's quicker than me but he's still on his first year. The seniors like Priya will be fine for a while, because someone has to check what the machine writes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used the assistant. Would you hold out, or give in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give in, but only a little, and I'd hate it. I'd use the assistant for writing tests, which is the dullest bit anyway. If giving in a little is what keeps me employed, I'll do it and complain about it at the union meeting.

say: I'd say job cuts from AI are a **company choice**, not bad weather.
I'd push for **rules** that protect training and require consultation before cuts.
think: I'm the **obvious one** to cut: junior, slow and refusing the tool.
If juniors stop being hired, the **next cut** lands on me.
do: Push the union group for a **written agreement** on training and notice.
Learn the **assistant** just enough to stop being the odd one out by summer.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit **angry** that the quiet, logical work is being taken.
S1.quote: I'm junior, I'm slower than average, and I'm the only one who won't use the tool. If they stop hiring juniors and one of us goes, it's me.
fieldNote: She names herself as the **first cut** with no hesitation.
Her response is **collective** first and personal second.
She'll accept the tool only **grudgingly**, for the dullest tasks.
Strong savings give her **time**, but she has no next career in mind.

steps.text: Ask the union group to demand a written training and notice agreement
Use the coding assistant for writing tests by summer
Move the holiday fund into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud, at work and online: this is going to wreck people, and the government has to step in now. I'd be the one sharing petitions for a jobs guarantee and a tax on the companies selling it. I wouldn't be polite about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is gone, probably within a year of it arriving. Everything I do is at a screen. There's no version of me, slow and junior, that a company keeps when the machine does it better and cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the nursing degree at the city college straight away, for the autumn after next. I'd keep working at Routewise as long as they'd pay me and save nearly all of it. And I'd campaign with the union for a basic income, because a degree won't save everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the speed of it. Two years isn't enough to change careers, it's barely enough to finish a course, and I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that gap mean anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the only thing that gives me any hope. Nursing is hands-on, so I'd get three more years than in software, but I'd be swapping one cliff for a slightly further one. Three years isn't a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner Ines the night you decided?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm coming to her world, and ask if she can stand me at home talking about wards. She'd laugh, then she'd go quiet, because her hospital might not survive robots either. We'd have one income for a while and we'd have to be careful.

say: I'd say the **government** must step in before this wrecks people.
I'd share petitions for a **jobs guarantee** and a tax on AI sellers.
think: My **screen job** is gone within about a year of AGI arriving.
No firm keeps a **slow junior** when the machine is better and cheaper.
do: Apply for the **nursing degree** at the city college for next autumn.
Stay at Routewise and **save** nearly all of the pay.
Campaign with the union for a **basic income**.
feel: **Alarmed** by the speed, lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: Nursing is hands-on, so I'd get three more years than in software, but I'd be swapping one cliff for a slightly further one.
fieldNote: She sees the robot gap as **borrowed time**, not safety.
Her partner's work points her towards **nursing**.
Politics is a **first move**, not an afterthought, for her.
One **income** for a while is a real cost she names.

steps.text: Apply for the city college nursing degree for next autumn
Bank nearly all of the Routewise pay until the job ends
Campaign with the union for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much the same as before: this needs rules and a safety net, and we should build them now while there's time. I'd say that at union meetings and I'd say it to my manager. Five years is long enough that nobody can claim they were surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my coding job lasts maybe three or four years, and then it's gone. The difference is I can actually finish something before it goes. That changes it from a panic to a plan, even if I don't like the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the part-time nursing course next year and keep coding three days a week to pay for it. I'd ask Priya to put me on the services that are hardest to replace, so I last longer. I'd keep saving and keep going to union meetings about the transition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than with two years. It still hurts, because I worked hard for a job I'm not great at yet. But I'd have time to become good at something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with the two-year version, what do the extra three years buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A degree, basically. Nursing takes about three years, so I'd finish around 2030, before the AGI and a few years before the robots. It's not forever, but it's a real job in a real place with real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to make that plan work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, the car, and probably moving to a cheaper flat. My partner Ines would carry more of the rent for a while. I'd hate that, but we've always said we'd take turns.

say: I'd say we should build **rules** and a **safety net** while there's still time.
I'd tell my manager nobody can claim **surprise** with five years' warning.
think: My coding job lasts about **three or four years**.
Five years turns a **panic** into a plan I can finish.
do: Start a **part-time nursing** course next year.
Keep coding **three days** a week to pay for it.
Keep going to **union meetings** about the transition.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, and sad to leave a job she's still learning.
S3.quote: Nursing takes about three years, so I'd finish around 2030, before the AGI and a few years before the robots.
fieldNote: The extra years make her plan **finishable**, which lowers her fear.
She'd ask to work on the **hardest-to-replace** code to buy time.
She accepts leaning on her **partner's income** as fair turn-taking.
Her sadness is about leaving a craft she never **mastered**.

steps.text: Start the part-time nursing course next year
Drop to three coding days a week to fund study
Keep attending union meetings on the AI transition

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for doing it badly. I'd push for retraining money for everyone, not only the clever ones. Publicly I'd sound almost hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably still end up out of software, just later. I'd be 37 when the AGI arrives. That's young enough to start again, but old enough to be tired of starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep coding for now and actually get good at it, because I'd have time to. I'd save hard for five years so I could afford to retrain later without stress. And I'd stay active in the union, because the rules get written in the quiet years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow, low way, like a bill you know is coming. Not frightening, just always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A decade is long. Would you still leave software, or try to ride it out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ride it out for five or six years and then go. Leaving too early wastes the pay, and leaving too late means competing with everyone else who waited. Somewhere around 2031 I'd start the nursing course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about children? Does this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. My partner Ines and I talked about children in our thirties. I'd want to be through the career switch before then, so it might push that back.

say: I'd say a decade leaves **no excuse** for doing this badly.
I'd push for **retraining money** for everyone, not only the clever ones.
think: I'd still end up **out of software**, just later.
At **37** I could restart, but I'd be tired of restarting.
do: Stay in coding and finally get **good at it** while there's time.
Save hard for **five years** to fund a later switch.
feel: A slow, **low anxiety**, like a bill she knows is coming.
S4.quote: I'd be 37 when the AGI arrives. That's young enough to start again, but old enough to be tired of starting again.
fieldNote: She'd time her exit to avoid the **crowd** of late switchers.
The long warning pushes back her **children** plans.
She sees the quiet years as when **rules** get written.
Her worry stays steady rather than **sharp**.

steps.text: Get properly skilled on the routing code over two years
Save hard for five years to fund a later switch
Push children back until after the career switch

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years is no time to switch careers, and I'm the kind of person who needs time. What would help is paid retraining with a living wage, run by the public, not by the companies selling the AI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why I won't use the tools. It isn't fear of technology, I write software. I just think if I hand over the thinking, I'll never get good, and I'd rather be slow and real than fast and hollow.

headlineQuote: If I hand over the thinking, I'll never get good, and I'd rather be slow and real than fast and hollow.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old** junior Java developer at a route-planning software firm, careful but slower than her peers.
She has never used an **AI assistant**, on principle, and resents the pressure to start.
Union-minded, she reaches for **rules and safety nets** before personal escape plans.
Her savings give her **time**; her partner's nursing work points her towards a hands-on second career.
She gets calmer as the warning time grows, because a **nursing degree** becomes finishable.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too little time to change careers.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with a living wage, run publicly rather than by AI sellers.
